strengths: RegCache addresses an important computer-vision deployment problem: activation outliers in pretrained vision encoders. The training-free combination of cached registers, selective insertion, and token deletion is a useful adaptation of prefix-based quantization to vision. Relevant prior work on prefix quantization and test-time registers is acknowledged and compared.

The strongest empirical gains are substantial. In Table 2, RegCache improves W6A6 RepQ-ViT accuracy from 53.25% to 66.73% for CLIP and from 46.51% to 68.35% for OpenCLIP; SigLIP2 with PTQ4ViT improves from 41.54% to 68.17%. These demonstrate value beyond improving naive quantization.

Evaluation covers five encoder families, several quantization methods, classification, and image–text retrieval. Transferring ImageNet-selected registers to four other classification datasets provides useful evidence that the method does not merely fit its search task.

Layerwise sensitivity analysis, reductions in activation norms, insertion-layer experiments, and comparison with test-time registers provide complementary support for the approach. The paper also explicitly acknowledges its model-specific hyperparameter search.
weaknesses: The strongest-baseline experiments require verification. Table 8 reverses the CLIP/OpenCLIP full-precision accuracies relative to Table 2. FIMA-Q achieves essentially full-precision SigLIP/SigLIP2 classification accuracy at every bitwidth, including W4A4, without explaining this striking difference from the other baselines. In Table 9, several SigLIP2 FIMA-Q retrieval entries exactly match SigLIP entries despite different full-precision performance. These are not proof of invalid experiments, but collectively undermine confidence in the comparisons with the most competitive baseline.

The ablation interpretation contradicts Table 6. The text claims either component alone performs worse than the baseline, yet caching alone improves SigLIP from 69.71% to 74.37%, almost matching the combined 74.38%; deletion alone improves SigLIP2 from 26.04% to 69.06%. Thus, complementary necessity is not established across models. Component ablations with stronger quantizers, additional encoders, and independently tuned component settings are needed to establish which changes drive the gains.

Important reproducibility details are missing: selected insertion layers and prefix/deletion counts per configuration, the deletion search range, reference-task evaluation size, cache precision, and exact quantized operations. The method also alternates between identifying tokens at the sensitive FC2 input and deleting them at the block input without clearly explaining how these locations are reconciled. DINOv2's reported 'zero-shot' classification protocol needs specification because the encoder has no native text classifier.

The search uses 50,000 reference images and task-accuracy-based selection, whereas baseline calibration uses much smaller sample sets. This is a legitimate resource tradeoff, but matched-data or matched-search-budget controls are missing. The one-hour search estimate covers naive pseudo-quantization rather than the stronger methods, and sensitivity to reference-pool size or random sampling is not reported.

The mechanistic and generality claims exceed the evidence. High cosine similarity at FC2 inputs, especially when explained by a shared dominant coordinate, does not establish interchangeability of the corresponding attention keys and values. Figure 8 supports insertion before the sensitive layer but shows similar performance for early insertion, so middle-layer insertion is principally supported as an efficiency choice. Experiments use base-sized models and global tasks; applicability to dense prediction after deleting spatial tokens remains untested.

Practical efficiency remains incompletely demonstrated. The experiments specify dynamic quantization despite motivating static quantization, and Table 12 does not establish real integer-kernel speedups against full precision or edge-device performance. All reported wall-clock times increase, including approximately 5–6% for CLIP/OpenCLIP, so the statement that cost decreases on average needs qualification. These concerns, together with the experimental inconsistencies, leave a slight preference for rejection despite the promising main results.

strengths: RegCache addresses a relevant problem: activation outliers can severely degrade quantized pretrained vision encoders. Its training-free combination of cached middle-layer registers and token deletion is a plausible, useful adaptation of attention-sink prefixing to vision. The paper appropriately acknowledges related register and LLM quantization methods.

The reported improvements are substantial in several meaningful settings. In Table 2, RegCache improves W6A6 RepQ-ViT from 53.25% to 66.73% on CLIP and from 46.51% to 68.35% on OpenCLIP; W6A6 PTQ4ViT on SigLIP2 improves from 41.54% to 68.17%. These gains demonstrate potential beyond merely repairing naive quantization.

The evaluation covers five encoder families, multiple quantization methods, classification, and image–text retrieval. Transfer of ImageNet-derived prefixes to four additional classification datasets provides useful evidence that the cached registers are not exclusively effective on the search dataset. Supplementary comparisons with test-time registers and rotation-based quantization strengthen the empirical scope.

The layerwise sensitivity analysis and measured reductions in activation norms provide an interpretable motivation for the method. The manuscript also explicitly acknowledges the need for encoder- and quantizer-specific hyperparameter selection.
weaknesses: Important implementation and evaluation details remain unresolved. Section 4.3 describes deletion at the input of the sensitive block, but Equation (2) selects tokens using the input to the sensitive layer, which is generally FC2 inside that block. These are different representations and execution points. The manuscript also omits the deletion-count search range, selected configurations, cached-KV precision and quantization handling, and a clear account of how candidate tokens are tracked across layers. DINOv2 is reported under 'zero-shot' classification without explaining the classifier or evaluation protocol. These omissions impede reproduction of the central results.

The strongest recent-baseline evidence needs verification. Table 8 reverses the CLIP/OpenCLIP full-precision accuracies relative to Table 2. It also reports almost identical full-precision and FIMA-Q accuracies for SigLIP and SigLIP2 across W4A4, W6A6, and W8A8, despite the severe low-bit degradation of other methods. Table 9 contains repeated SigLIP/SigLIP2 FIMA-Q baseline values across different model/bitwidth settings. These patterns do not establish an implementation error, but require corrected tables and explicit quantization-coverage details before the comparison can be confidently interpreted.

The interpretation of the component ablation is contradicted by Table 6. The text claims either component alone performs worse than the baseline, yet caching alone improves SigLIP from 69.71% to 74.37%, and deletion alone improves SigLIP2 from 26.04% to 69.06%. On SigLIP, adding deletion to caching contributes only 0.01 percentage points. Thus, the evidence supports model-dependent roles rather than the claimed general synergy. Ablations with stronger quantizers, random or ordinary-token caches, and matched hyperparameter search would better isolate the contribution of curated universal registers.

The deployment motivation is only partially supported. Section 5.1 evaluates dynamic activation quantization despite the introduction emphasizing obstacles to static quantization. Appendix H reports FLOPs estimated through pseudo-quantization and whole-validation-set timings, without establishing native low-bit execution or speedup over full precision. All reported latencies increase with RegCache. This does not invalidate an Algorithms/General contribution, but it leaves the practical benefit for real-time edge inference unverified.

The universality and necessity claims exceed the evidence. High FC2 cosine similarity can follow simply from a shared dominant coordinate, as Appendix B itself proves; it does not establish that the corresponding KV representations are semantically interchangeable. The foreground-masking experiment also changes image statistics, so it does not uniquely establish the proposed semantic explanation. Empirically, Table 2 shows degradation for every DINOv2 W8A8 baseline, and Table 8 shows small SigLIP2 declines with FIMA-Q. Cross-dataset transfer is tested only against naive quantization, and all evaluated encoders are base-sized.

The additional search budget is substantial relative to the stated baseline calibration sets: RegCache curates candidates from 50,000 training images and repeatedly selects configurations using classification accuracy. The exact selection-set size, label requirements, sensitivity to reference sampling, and benefit under matched data/search budgets are not established. Together with the reporting inconsistencies and incomplete specification, this leaves important concerns that favor weak rejection despite the promising accuracy gains.

strengths: RegCache addresses an important problem in vision-encoder activation quantization. Assessed as an Algorithms/General contribution, its combination of cached middle-layer registers and token deletion is a meaningful adaptation of prefix-based outlier mitigation to vision transformers. The paper appropriately acknowledges related work on registers, attention sinks, and LLM prefixing.

The main experiments demonstrate substantial improvements over established quantization methods. In Table 2, RegCache improves RepQ-ViT W6A6 accuracy from 53.25% to 66.73% on CLIP and from 46.51% to 68.35% on OpenCLIP; SigLIP2 with PTQ4ViT improves from 41.54% to 68.17%. These gains support the practical value of the approach without requiring a new standalone quantizer.

Evaluation spans five encoder families, several quantizers, classification, and image–text retrieval. Table 4 also demonstrates transfer of ImageNet-derived prefixes to four other classification datasets. The comparison against test-time registers in Table 14 helps distinguish the contribution from closely related work.

The empirical analysis provides a coherent motivation: quantization sensitivity coincides with activation outliers, outlier tokens exhibit high cross-image similarity, and RegCache substantially reduces maximum activation norms. The paper also explicitly acknowledges the need for model-specific hyperparameter selection.
weaknesses: Important implementation and evaluation details remain unspecified. The manuscript does not report the selected insertion layers, prefix counts, deletion counts, or deletion search range for individual configurations. Sections 4.1–4.3 also alternate between FC2-input activations and block-input tokens when defining selection and deletion, leaving the precise operation unclear. Cached KV precision and its treatment in attention quantization are not specified. Finally, the DINOv2 results are described as zero-shot classification without explaining the classifier or evaluation protocol for this image-only encoder.

The supplementary results contain discrepancies that require verification, particularly because they support compatibility with the recent FIMA-Q baseline. Table 8 reverses the CLIP/OpenCLIP full-precision values relative to Table 2. Table 9 reports SigLIP2 FIMA-Q retrieval numbers that closely reproduce SigLIP's numbers across bitwidths. Table 8 also reports essentially unchanged full-precision accuracy for SigLIP and SigLIP2 even at W4A4, without explaining this striking difference from the other quantizers. These observations do not establish an implementation error, but the strongest low-bit evidence needs an auditable explanation.

The ablation interpretation overstates the evidence. Section 5.2 claims that either component alone performs worse than the baseline, but Table 6 shows prefix caching improving SigLIP from 69.71% to 74.37%, and deletion improving SigLIP2 from 26.04% to 69.06%. Adding deletion to caching contributes only 0.01 percentage points on SigLIP. Thus, the results support architecture-dependent roles rather than a general requirement for both components. Ablations across more encoders and quantizers, with a full-precision RegCache control, would better isolate the source of improvement.

The deployment motivation is stronger than the systems evidence. Experiments use dynamic per-tensor quantization, despite motivating static activation quantization. Appendix H reports simulated-quantization FLOPs and whole-validation-set timings, without establishing an actual integer inference speedup over full precision or specifying a sufficiently detailed timing setup. Every reported latency increases with RegCache, including roughly 5–6% for CLIP/OpenCLIP; the suggestion that hardware caching readily eliminates this cost is untested.

Claims of consistently improved performance need qualification. All three non-naive DINOv2 W8A8 baselines worsen in Table 2, and some retrieval metrics also decline. Most main-table W4A4 configurations remain severely degraded despite improvement. The broader transfer results use only the naive baseline, and all evaluated encoders are base-sized. These limits do not erase the substantial W6A6 gains, but together with the unresolved protocol and result-reporting issues, they leave a slight preference for rejection.

strengths: RegCache addresses a relevant computer-vision deployment problem: activation outliers that impair low-bit quantization of pretrained vision encoders. As an Algorithms/General contribution, its training-free combination of cached registers, middle-layer insertion, and residual outlier-token deletion is practical and technically motivated.

The empirical evaluation is broad, spanning five encoder families, five PTQ baselines, multiple bitwidths, classification, retrieval, and image/video VLM tasks. Several improvements are substantial: Table 2 raises CLIP W4A4 accuracy from 50.41% to 62.08% with FIMA-Q and from 1.56% to 46.07% with ERQ. Improvements therefore extend beyond the naive quantization baseline.

The analysis connects layerwise quantization sensitivity with outlier emergence, measures cross-image similarity of outlier tokens, and verifies reductions in activation magnitude. Table 8 usefully demonstrates that caching and deletion have different effects across architectures and can complement each other.

The supplementary experiments meaningfully strengthen the case: comparison with test-time registers, label-free reconstruction-based selection, transfer to additional datasets, segmentation with interpolation, and compatibility with rotation and weight-only quantization. Related register and LLM-prefixing methods are explicitly acknowledged.

TensorRT measurements provide evidence that the additional operations need not erase INT8 inference benefits: Table 6 reports approximately 1–1.5% overhead for standalone encoders. The limitations section also appropriately acknowledges architecture-specific hyperparameter tuning.
weaknesses: Important implementation details remain ambiguous. Section 4 identifies the sensitive layer through FC2 inputs, but Section 4.3 describes deletion at the input of the containing transformer block while Equation (2) selects tokens using the sensitive-layer activations. These are different execution points. The paper should specify the exact ordering, whether identifying tokens requires additional computation, how candidate positions are tracked to obtain per-layer KV caches, the cache precision, and the selected insertion/deletion counts and deletion search range.

The quantization and evaluation protocols need greater precision. Appendix E describes all baselines as using per-tensor dynamic quantization, despite their method-specific quantizers and the introduction's emphasis on static activation quantization. The quantized operations, exceptions, and adaptations should be enumerated. DINOv2 is included under 'zero-shot' classification without explaining its classification head or evaluation protocol, and the precision of the language model in the VLM accuracy experiments is unclear.

The strongest mechanistic claims exceed the evidence. High cosine similarity of FC2 outliers can follow from shared dominant channels, as Appendix F itself shows, but does not establish semantic meaninglessness or universal interchangeability of their attention keys and values. The foreground-masking experiment is suggestive but also changes image statistics. Random-token, normal-token, and alternative cache-construction controls would better establish why curated registers work.

Claims of consistent improvement across all setups should be narrowed. Table 2 shows degradation for every evaluated non-naive DINOv2 baseline at W8A8, and FIMA-Q on SigLIP2 declines at all three bitwidths. Some retrieval results also decrease. The component ablation covers only two models under naive W8A8 quantization, so it does not establish which components drive the headline low-bit improvements with stronger PTQ methods. Repeated searches or uncertainty estimates would help interpret small gains.

The deployment evidence is narrower than the low-bit accuracy claims. Latency is measured at INT8, whereas the most prominent accuracy gains and VLM results use 4-bit quantization. Standalone timing uses batch size 64, with no FP16 comparison or batch-one measurement. The reported search cost is for naive RTN, despite using 50,000 reference images and baseline-dependent searches. These omissions limit conclusions about practical cost, although they do not negate the accuracy results.

strengths: RegCache addresses a relevant computer vision problem: activation outliers that impair low-bit quantization of pretrained vision encoders. Assessed as an Algorithms/General contribution, its combination of cached visual registers, intermediate-layer insertion, and token deletion is a useful adaptation of prior attention-sink methods.

The empirical evaluation is broad, covering five encoder families, five PTQ baselines, classification, retrieval, and image/video VLM benchmarks. Several gains are substantial: Table 2 improves CLIP W4A4 accuracy from 50.41% to 62.08% with FIMA-Q and from 1.56% to 46.07% with ERQ. Improvements therefore extend beyond the naive quantization baseline.

The supporting analyses connect quantization sensitivity with outlier emergence and demonstrate considerable reductions in activation magnitude. Table 8 also establishes that caching and deletion have different, complementary effects across SigLIP and SigLIP2.

The supplementary material addresses several practical concerns rather than relying solely on ImageNet results: it includes comparison with test-time registers, transfer to other datasets, label-free reconstruction-based selection, segmentation with interpolation, and combinations with rotation and weight-only quantization. Prior register and prefixing approaches are appropriately acknowledged.
weaknesses: Important implementation details remain ambiguous. Sections 3–4 identify candidates using FC2-input activations, but Section 4.2 and Figure 5 do not clearly explain how the corresponding per-layer keys and values are recovered, particularly for insertion before the candidate-selection layer. Section 4.3 describes deletion at the block input while Equation (2) selects tokens at the sensitive layer input. An explicit algorithm should resolve the execution order and specify cache precision, selected layers, deletion counts, and prefix counts for each configuration.

The evaluation protocol is insufficiently specified in consequential places. Appendix E describes all baselines as using per-tensor dynamic quantization, whereas static activation quantization motivates the method. The manuscript should clarify which tensors and operations are quantized, how cached prefixes are handled, and whether the accuracy and TensorRT experiments use matching configurations. The classifier used for DINOv2's reported 'zero-shot' ImageNet accuracy and the handling of deleted spatial tokens in Qwen3-VL also need explanation.

The calibration and search burden is understated. Candidate curation uses 50,000 ImageNet training images, followed by task-based hyperparameter searches, while several PTQ baselines use only 32 calibration examples. The approximately one-hour search cost is reported only for naive RTN. Data-budget sensitivity, complete search costs for stronger baselines, and variation across reference-image samples would better substantiate the lightweight deployment claim. Appendix K reduces dependence on labels but does not fully resolve these concerns.

Some generality claims exceed the results. Table 2 shows degradation for every evaluated non-naive DINOv2 W8A8 baseline, including 82.27% to 81.55% with RepQ-ViT and 71.46% to 70.38% with NoisyQuant. SigLIP2 with FIMA-Q also declines across bit widths. These exceptions do not negate the substantial gains elsewhere, but claims of improvement across all setups should be narrowed, and uncertainty estimates are needed to interpret small gains.

The efficiency evidence is narrower than the main accuracy story. Table 6 measures INT8 latency, whereas the headline gains and VLM evaluations emphasize 4-bit quantization. It supports low overhead in the tested INT8 configurations but does not establish practical W4A4 acceleration. Input resolutions, video lengths, cache/deletion settings, timing variability, and deployed accuracy would make the efficiency results more interpretable.

The mechanistic interpretation remains suggestive. High cosine similarity dominated by shared extreme coordinates does not establish semantic meaninglessness or interchangeability of attention keys and values, and zeroing backgrounds changes image statistics as well as semantic content. Comparisons against random, ordinary-token, and simpler averaged caches under matched search budgets would better isolate the value of outlier-based curation. Nevertheless, the breadth and magnitude of the demonstrated gains support a slight preference for acceptance.

strengths: Assessed as an Algorithms/General contribution, RegCache offers a useful training-free adaptation of register caching to vision-encoder quantization. Middle-layer insertion and residual sink-token deletion address vision-specific behavior, and the method complements existing PTQ algorithms.

The empirical evaluation is broad, covering five encoder families, five PTQ baselines, multiple bitwidths, classification, retrieval, and image/video VLM benchmarks. Several improvements are substantial: on W4A4 CLIP, FIMA-Q improves from 50.41% to 62.08%, and ERQ improves from 1.56% to 46.07% (Table 2).

The supporting analyses connect quantization sensitivity to activation outliers, demonstrate reduced activation ranges, and examine the complementary effects of caching and deletion. Comparison with test-time registers in Appendix B helps establish value relative to closely related work.

Transfer to other classification datasets and COCO retrieval supports the usefulness of ImageNet-derived registers beyond their selection task. The reconstruction-loss selection variant in Appendix K is particularly valuable because it reduces dependence on labeled reference data.

TensorRT measurements provide practical evidence that RegCache adds little overhead to INT8 inference in the tested settings. Overall, the breadth and magnitude of the demonstrated gains support acceptance despite the limitations below.
weaknesses: Important implementation details remain insufficiently specified. Section 4.3 describes deletion at the input of the sensitive block, whereas Equation 2 uses the input of the sensitive layer, typically FC2; these are different locations. The manuscript should clarify how selected token positions map to cached K/V states, cache precision and quantization, the deletion search range, and the final configurations. Handling deleted tokens in VLM spatial merging also needs explanation.

The quantization and evaluation protocols need clarification. Appendix E describes all baselines as using per-tensor dynamic quantization, while the motivation emphasizes static activation quantization and several baselines use specialized quantizers. Exact quantized operations and precision exceptions should be reported. DINOv2 is included under 'zero-shot classification' without explaining its classification head or evaluation protocol.

Claims of improvement across all setups exceed the evidence. For DINOv2 at W8A8, every reported non-naive baseline declines, with an average loss of 0.47 points; SigLIP2 with FIMA-Q also declines slightly. Table 3 contains retrieval regressions. These exceptions do not negate the strong overall results, but claims should be qualified, and repeated selection/calibration runs would help interpret small differences.

The mechanistic explanation is suggestive rather than conclusive. High cosine similarity can follow from shared dominant coordinates, as Appendix F itself demonstrates, without establishing semantic meaninglessness or interchangeable K/V behavior. Zeroing backgrounds also changes low-level image statistics. The empirical utility is stronger than the causal account of why universal registers emerge.

Practical efficiency is demonstrated only for INT8, whereas the strongest accuracy motivation concerns 4-bit quantization. Standalone timing uses batch size 64, leaving low-batch and edge deployment uncertain. The method also curates candidates from 50,000 images and tunes configurations per encoder and PTQ method; the reported one-hour search cost covers naive RTN rather than the full range of baselines.

The relationship to prior cached test-time registers deserves sharper isolation. Appendix B acknowledges that the closest method already supports KV-cache register injection, but compares only two encoders under naive W8A8. Controlled comparisons using the same search budget and PTQ backbone would better distinguish the benefits of candidate curation, middle-layer placement, and deletion.
